lead: Most axial members have just enough supports for equilibrium to find every reaction. A statically indeterminate axial member has more unknown reactions than equilibrium equations. The extra equation comes from compatibility: the fixed ends force the total elongation to a known value, often zero. Engineers meet this in continuous pipes, fixed-end rods, preloaded bolts and composite ties. The method combines equilibrium, compatibility and δ=FL/(AE) to find the real reactions, then checks them against the applied load.
prereq: You need: axial deformation δ=FL/(AE) and compound-bar strain sharing from Chapter 1.6, plus free-body equilibrium.

blocks.text: An axial member is determinate when equilibrium alone finds every reaction. One unknown, one equation ΣF=0, done. It is statically indeterminate when the number of independent unknown reactions is greater than the number of independent equilibrium equations. For a straight axial member there is one equilibrium equation along the axis. A bar fixed at both ends has two axial reactions, so its degree of indeterminacy is 2 − 1 = 1. Degree of indeterminacy = unknowns − equilibrium equations. Continuous rails, pipes anchored at two walls and rods with end plates often fall in this class.

Equilibrium still holds. For a fixed-fixed bar it gives R_A + R_B = P, one equation for two reactions. The missing equation is geometric: both ends are fixed, so the total change in length is set, often zero. That is compatibility. In the linear elastic range, superposition is allowed: add the displacement caused by the load and the displacement caused by the redundant reaction.

Use a sign convention before writing equations. Take elongation positive and the axis positive to the right. Define the redundant as the extra unknown reaction (or internal force) removed to make the member determinate; compatibility then finds it. Remove one support, say the right one, and let the bar stretch freely under P. Compute the displacement at the cut by adding δ=FL/(AE) over the segments from the fixed end to the cut. Use each segment's own length, area, E and internal force. Here δ is elongation in m, F is internal axial force in N, L is segment length in m, A is area in m² and E is Young's modulus in Pa. Segments beyond the cut do not contribute when they carry no load. For the worked example below, after freeing B, segment CB carries no force, so δ_P=P a/(AE). Put back the redundant reaction R and compute the signed displacement δ_R it alone causes at the same point. Compatibility says the real cut point does not move: δ_P + δ_R = 0, with both terms signed in the same positive direction. If the redundant opposes δ_P, δ_R is negative. If you work with magnitudes only, write δ_P = δ_R. Solve for R, then use equilibrium for the other reaction. This is the method of consistent deformations.

items: Draw the free body and count unknown reactions.
Remove one support and find the free displacement δ_P at the cut as ΣFL/(AE) over the segments from the fixed end to the cut, using each segment's internal force.
Apply the redundant reaction R and find the signed displacement δ_R at the same cut.
Set δ_P + δ_R = 0 and solve for R; with magnitudes only, set δ_P = δ_R.
Back-substitute in equilibrium for the other reaction.

blocks.text: For a uniform bar of area A and length L, fixed at both ends, load P at distance a from the left end and b=L−a from the right end, the reaction magnitudes are R_L = P b/L and R_R = P a/L. R_L and R_R act opposite to P. Derivation: segment AC elongates by R_L a/(AE); segment CB shortens by R_R b/(AE); compatibility gives R_L a/(AE) − R_R b/(AE)=0, so R_L a = R_R b. Combine with R_L+R_R=P. E and A cancel because the bar is uniform; they do not cancel for a stepped bar.

Parallel rods are another indeterminate case. A rigid block hangs from two vertical rods of the same length but different areas. Assume the block is guided to remain horizontal, or the load is applied so that it does not rotate; then both rods have the same elongation. Equilibrium gives F1+F2=P, where F1 and F2 are rod forces and P is the hanging load. Compatibility gives the same elongation: F1 L/(A1 E1)=F2 L/(A2 E2), where A1 and A2 are areas and E1 and E2 are Young's moduli. If E is equal, F1/F2=A1/A2: the stiffer rod takes more load. A thick tie in a parallel set can carry more than a thin one of the same length.

Run three checks. First, reactions must balance the applied load. Second, each segment's elongation must use that segment's length and internal force, not the full bar. Third, signs must match the chosen convention: tension positive, compression negative. A negative answer means the reaction acts opposite to your assumed arrow. Thermal loading, where a temperature change adds a free strain, is handled in Chapter 1.8. Indeterminate beams use the same compatibility idea; see Unit 5, Deflection of Beams and Energy Methods.

figure.caption: The flow shows equilibrium, compatibility and force-displacement leading to reactions; in the worked example the reactions are 20 kN and 10 kN.

spec.title: Indeterminate axial bar
spec.aria: Equilibrium gives one equation, compatibility gives another, and the axial force-displacement relation lets us solve the reactions.

examples.question: A uniform prismatic bar AB is fixed at both ends. Its length is L=1.5 m, area A=300 mm² and E=200 GPa. An axial load P=30 kN acts to the right at point C, 0.5 m from the left end A. Find the reactions at A and B.
steps: Take elongation positive and the axis positive to the right. Let R_A and R_B be reaction magnitudes at A and B, both assumed to act to the left, opposite P.
Equilibrium along the axis: R_A + R_B = P = 30 kN.
Segment AC has length a=0.5 m and internal force N_AC = R_A (tension). Segment CB has length b=1.5−0.5=1.0 m and internal force N_CB = −R_B (compression).
AE = (300×10⁻⁶ m²)(200×10⁹ Pa) = 6.0×10⁷ N. It cancels. Elongations: δ_AC = R_A(0.5)/(AE) and δ_CB = −R_B(1.0)/(AE), with lengths in m and forces in N after unit conversion.
Compatibility of the fixed ends: δ_AC + δ_CB = 0 → 0.5 R_A − 1.0 R_B = 0 → R_A = 2 R_B.
Substitute in equilibrium: 2R_B + R_B = 30 kN → R_B = 10 kN; R_A = 20 kN.
examples.answer: R_A = 20 kN and R_B = 10 kN, both acting to the left; their sum is 30 kN.
examples.check:
P=30.0
L=1.5
a=0.5
b=L-a
R_L=P*b/L
R_R=P*a/L
print(R_L)
print(R_R)
print(R_L+R_R)

traps: Compatibility is about total elongation between fixed points, not about equal reactions. In a uniform fixed-fixed bar the reaction split depends on load position, not on E or A.
A sign slip is fatal: choose tension positive, keep it through every segment, and write δ_AC+δ_CB=0 for two fixed ends.
Use the segment length and the internal force in that segment. Using L=1.5 m for both segments in the example gives wrong answers.
Check R_L+R_R=P. If the reactions do not add to the applied axial load, equilibrium or arithmetic is wrong.
E and A cancel only when the whole bar has the same E and A. For a stepped bar, use ΣFL/(AE) and do not cancel.

quiz.q: Define degree of indeterminacy for an axial member.
quiz.a: Degree = number of independent unknown axial reactions minus number of independent axial equilibrium equations; a bar fixed at both ends with one axial load has degree 1.

quiz.q: Why does a fixed-fixed bar need compatibility?
quiz.a: Equilibrium gives R_A+R_B=P only; compatibility adds that total elongation between fixed ends is zero, giving a second equation for two reactions.

quiz.q: A uniform bar L=2.0 m fixed at both ends carries P=40 kN at 0.5 m from the left end. Find the reactions.
quiz.a: a=0.5 m, b=1.5 m. R_L=P b/L=40×1.5/2=30 kN, R_R=P a/L=40×0.5/2=10 kN; both opposite the load.

quiz.q: Two vertical rods have the same length and E, areas A and 2A, and hang from a rigid support carrying a rigid block of weight W. Find the force ratio and explain.
quiz.a: Same elongation gives F1 L/(A E)=F2 L/(2A E), so F1/F2=1/2; rod 2 carries twice the force because it is twice as stiff.

quiz.q: A bar has three axial reactions and one equilibrium equation. What is its degree of indeterminacy?
Why do E and A cancel in the reactions of a uniform fixed-fixed bar?
quiz.a: Both segment elongations have the same factor 1/(AE), so compatibility reduces to R_L a = R_R b; E and A affect deflection and stress, not the reaction split when uniform.

quiz.q: A fixed-fixed bar has δ_AC as elongation of AC and δ_CB as signed elongation of CB (tension positive). Why is δ_AC−δ_CB=0 wrong, and when is δ_AC−δ_CB=0 correct?
quiz.a: With signed elongation, δ_CB is negative in compression, so δ_AC−δ_CB adds magnitudes; compatibility is δ_AC+δ_CB=0. If δ_CB is taken as a positive compression magnitude, then δ_AC−δ_CB=0 is correct.

beyond: Not for the exam. In design offices, fixed-ended axial members appear in restrained pipework, preloaded bolted joints, rail tracks and composite strengthening plates. Software such as finite-element packages solves the same three ideas at thousands of points: equilibrium, compatibility and a material law. Research on smart structures adds thermal and piezoelectric strains to compatibility. Search next for consistent deformations, redundant reactions, and thermal prestress in pipes.
